title: The Assassination of Martin Luther King, Jr. Part I
summary: Part one of a two-part Stuff You Should Know episode on the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. It covers King's rising prominence and growing criticism from both white and Black Americans, including the division between his nonviolence doctrine and Malcolm X's approach. It covers his opposition to the Vietnam War, the Poor People's Campaign, and the 1968 Memphis sanitation workers' strike, including the March 28 march that turned violent. It describes King's return to Memphis, his "I've Been to the Mountaintop" speech, the 1968 stabbing in Harlem by Izola Curry, the April 4 shooting at the Lorraine Motel, the evidence found at Bessie Brewer's boarding house, and the immediate aftermath: national mourning, uprisings in about 125 cities, Coretta Scott King's silent march, and the Atlanta funeral. Part two will cover the investigation and the path of the bullet. The hosts skip listener mail for this two-parter.
topics: I've Been to the Mountaintop speech
Coretta Scott King Memphis silent march

segments.title: Opening and two-parter setup
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the two-part episode on King's assassination and note there was much more to the story than they knew.

segments.title: King's rise to prominence
segments.summary: King rose to fame through the Montgomery bus boycott, appeared on Time magazine's cover, was named Time's Man of the Year in 1963, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

segments.title: Nonviolence versus Malcolm X
segments.summary: The hosts contrast King's nonviolence doctrine and integration goal with Malcolm X's black separatism and support for self-defense, and note King's growing criticism from Black Americans as well as white Americans.

segments.title: Vietnam stance, Riverside speech, and Poor People's Campaign
segments.summary: King became more vocal against the Vietnam War in 1967, including the Riverside Church speech, which drew heavy criticism and a break with LBJ. He then shifted focus to economic justice and launched the Poor People's Campaign, which drew opposition even from his own staff.

segments.title: Memphis in spring 1968
segments.summary: Memphis was tense because of the sanitation workers' strike, which King saw as a bridge between civil rights and economic justice for poor people of all races.

segments.title: Deaths of sanitation workers and the March 28 violent march
segments.summary: Two sanitation workers, Echol Cole and Robert Walker, were crushed to death in a truck malfunction, prompting a mass walkout. King led a march of about 5,000 on March 28 that turned violent when the Invaders group looted; police shot and killed 16-year-old Larry Payne, about 60 were injured, and Memphis was placed under curfew with National Guard deployed.

segments.title: King's return to Memphis and the Mountaintop speech
segments.summary: King insisted on returning to Memphis to redeem the march, canceling an Africa trip. In his April 3 Mason Temple speech, he recounted the 1958 stabbing by Izola Curry and spoke of seeing the Promised Land.
topics: I've Been to the Mountaintop speech

segments.title: Court injunction delays the march
segments.summary: A federal court injunction postponed the planned April 4 march to the following Monday. King met with the Invaders at the Lorraine Motel to negotiate nonviolence, and stayed in town for court appeals.

segments.title: The shooting at the Lorraine Motel
segments.summary: On the evening of April 4, King was shot on the balcony of room 306 at the Lorraine Motel, a Black-owned hotel, as he prepared for dinner at Reverend Billy Kyle's house. Shot at 6:01 pm, he was pronounced dead at 7:05 pm. Undercover officer Marrell McCollough was kneeling by him. The U2 song 'Pride' lyric was corrected in the hosts' discussion.

segments.title: Autopsy and evidence at Bessie Brewer's boarding house
segments.summary: The medical examiner Dr. Jerry T. Francisco found King died from a gunshot wound to the chin and neck, and did not fully dissect the bullet's path. Witnesses saw a man leave a bundle that contained a Remington 760 Game Master rifle, and scuff marks in the boarding house bathtub matched the shooting angle.

segments.title: National mourning and closures
segments.summary: Walter Cronkite reported the death on CBS, and LBJ declared April 7 a national day of mourning. Businesses closed, the NYSE closed on funeral day, and Roberto Clemente and Maury Wills led Pirates players to sit out MLB opening day.

segments.title: Uprisings after the assassination
segments.summary: Unrest spread to about 125 cities, with 39 people killed, about 3,500 injured, and federal troops deployed. Wilmington, Delaware was occupied by the National Guard for a year. The hosts situate the violence within the 1967 long hot summer and ongoing housing discrimination.

segments.title: Coretta Scott King's silent march in Memphis
segments.summary: Coretta Scott King led the planned silent march in Memphis on April 8 with her four children and about 40,000 people.

segments.title: Funeral, Sweet Auburn, and Lorraine Motel museum
segments.summary: King's funeral in Atlanta drew about 100,000 people; Benjamin Mays delivered the eulogy. The hosts describe the Sweet Auburn neighborhood, the King Center, and the Lorraine Motel's later preservation as the National Civil Rights Museum. Walter Bailey kept the motel open but left room 306 untouched, and Loria Bailey died five days after the shooting.

segments.title: Closing and listener mail skipped
segments.summary: The hosts say listener mail is skipped for two-parters, give a contact address, and sign off.
